If you don't know the answer, things just get heart breaking. But his open-book policy was something I liked, and I can say for sure that it helped me to learn the topics and not just memorize them for the exam.

Daniel frequently makes disrespectful and offensive remarks toward his co-instructor in front of the class, often in ways subtle enough to deny direct hostility, but still clearly inappropriate and disrespectful. Beyond this, his grading often feels unfair and inconsistent, which raises serious concerns about equity among students. During exams, cheating can go unnoticed, which further damages trust in the fairness of the course. In class discussions, Daniel tends to accept answers only when they match his exact expectations, while other valid perspectives are often ignored or dismissed, discouraging open participation. He also makes little effort to learn students’ names, which contributes to a sense of detachment. Additionally, there is an underlying pattern of condescension toward Turkish students that can feel subtly discriminatory, as though we are sometimes stereotyped or looked down upon as if we are peasants

Frankly speaking, I thoroughly enjoyed this course on Kant, but definitely not just because of Kant. Despite its complex subject matter (as you might know, Kant is a guy with different peculiarities), Professor Wolt's engaging teaching style in which we discussed everything and well-prepared weekly handouts made the content accessible and interesting, even for someone like me who isn't a philosophy major. Whether you're already interested in Kant or new to Kant's work, Professor Wolt's excellent communication skills as an instructor of this course ensure an enjoyable and enlightening experience for all students. Professor Wolt is also very open-minded about combining Kant's ideas with our own major in our term papers, even though they may not be closely related to each other; I suppose this is a really nice thing for non-Phil major students. So, I highly recommend this course and Professor Wolt, it's definitely due to Professor Wolt's exceptional teaching approach.

His feedback was really helpful and quite substantial; yet, one receives such feedbacks after they submit their work, despite the tutorials. He really reads the submitted work with great detail, which is fine, but the grade is not something that a grad student may disregard, despite how quality the feedback was. Even though you think that you have a good argument for your paper, you may still need to be careful about how you present your argument in a very detailed manner. This is good for academic writing in general and a good practice for a grad student, yet rather overwhelming if you are taking more than one class, which you probably will.

Unfortunately, I am on the fence about him. On the one hand, he is a top-notch instructor. By top-notch, I mean that he’s a perfect, immaculate lecturer. He is very helpful, knowledgeable, respectful, and thoughtful. Aristotle is hard to read, and he explains the texts very clearly. He prepares handouts and exercises to make the lectures more interesting. He listens to the questions and comes up with answers from the whole corpus. But on the other hand, more often than not, he gets frustrated very easily. Especially towards the end of the semester, it was customary to hear him say, “By now, I’m used to getting no answers from this group of people,” and see him look defeated in the face of the lack of contribution by the audience. I know this was not the best audience to teach Aristotle to. But I would have expected him not to take it that seriously — for one, it is unsettling to sit in the midst of an audience in which the lecturer claims to have given up all hope, and second, well, some students like to be there and while they are in class, they would like to learn as much as possible from this person. All in all, Bilkent is lucky to have him and should do everything not to lose him. If I could, I would have been glad to take the other courses he offers. I hope he’s happy no matter where he’s employed, I hope he has a fruitful academic career, and I hope his future audiences will fulfill his expectations — he most certainly deserves these.
